title: Dense Embeddings
description: See how the distributional hypothesis turns words into short dense vectors that encode meaning.
content:
One-hot vectors cannot express similarity. **Dense embeddings** fix this: every word becomes a short (50-1000 dimensional) vector in which geometric closeness encodes semantic relatedness.

The theoretical foundation is the **distributional hypothesis**: 'you shall know a word by the company it keeps' - words occurring in similar contexts have similar meanings. Count-based methods build a co-occurrence matrix, weight it (e.g., PPMI) and compress it with SVD; **prediction-based methods** learn the vectors directly:

> Word embedding models:
> • **Word2Vec Skip-gram** - predicts the surrounding context words from the center word; works well even for rare words
> • **Word2Vec CBOW** - predicts the center word from its surrounding context; faster to train
> • **Negative sampling** - instead of an expensive softmax over the whole vocabulary, learns to distinguish true (word, context) pairs from a few randomly sampled 'negative' words
> • **GloVe** - trained on global co-occurrence statistics, combining count-based and prediction-based ideas
> • **fastText** - represents words as bags of character n-grams, so rare and out-of-vocabulary words, even misspellings, still get vectors

The resulting vectors support algebraic analogies such as king - man + woman ≈ queen, and are evaluated intrinsically (similarity and analogy benchmarks, correlation with human judgments) and extrinsically (downstream task performance). Crucially, they are **static embeddings**: one vector per word type, so 'bank' has a single representation whether it denotes a river bank or a financial institution. **Contextual embeddings** (ELMo, BERT) produce a different vector for every occurrence, resolving polysemy.
